content:
# A Pre-Revenue AI Stack: Four Jobs, Four Free Tiers

For an established company, a free tier is a discount. For a pre-revenue startup, it is a runway decision. Every subscription that starts as free and converts to paid at month three is a cost the financial model did not include, and the conversion usually arrives at the least convenient moment — when usage grows, which is to say when the product starts working.

That makes the useful question different from a normal tool roundup. It is not which free tool is best in isolation, but which free tier survives long enough to matter, and what specifically ends it. A tool whose limit arrives at five users is worse than a slightly weaker tool whose limit arrives at five hundred.

## The four jobs a pre-revenue startup does

**Build the product.** Write the code, design the interface, run the infrastructure.

**Find the first customers.** Research the market, identify who has the problem, reach them.

**Look credible.** A name, a logo, a deck, a landing page. Investors and first customers judge quickly.

**Operate.** Notes, meetings, documentation, the unglamorous coordination that holds a small team together.

AI tools touch all four. The mistake is buying a paid plan in all four at once, which is how a pre-seed budget disappears into SaaS.

## Build the product without a budget

[[link:/tools/98|Lovable]] generates a full-stack application from a description, including database and authentication, with code you can export. For a founder validating an idea, that is a working prototype in a day instead of a month. The important property is the export: you are not locked in, so the generated code can become the real codebase if the idea survives.

[[link:/tools/494|v0 by Vercel]] does the same for interfaces. For a landing page or an internal dashboard, describing the layout and getting working components is faster than assembling a design system from scratch.

[[link:/tools/85|Replit AI]] combines generation with a hosted environment, so a prototype can be built, run and deployed without touching local setup. For a non-technical founder or a team without DevOps, that removes an entire category of blocker.

[[link:/tools/92|Hugging Face]] is where the free tier is genuinely generous because the models are open: hosted inference for testing, and the option to run the same model yourself later without renegotiating a contract. That portability is worth more to a startup than any feature.

[[link:/tools/93|LangChain]] is open source and free in the sense that matters. If the product involves retrieval or tool-calling, the framework you build on should not be a line item that grows with usage.

The limit that bites: generation credits. Prototyping is cheap; iterating on a live product with real users is not. Budget for the moment when the prototype becomes the product.

## Find the first customers

[[link:/tools/10|Perplexity AI]] is the fastest way to research a market with sources you can check. Who is already solving this, what the alternatives cost, what the objections are. Every answer carries citations, which matters when the conclusion feeds into a pitch.

[[link:/tools/6|ChatGPT]] handles the adjacent work: drafting outreach, rewriting a value proposition, preparing for the questions a customer will ask. Its weakness is the one that matters most here — it will produce confident copy about a customer it has never spoken to.

[[link:/tools/20|Claude]] is better when the input is long: a full set of customer interview transcripts, a competitor's documentation, a draft pitch. Its context window lets you work with the whole thing rather than excerpts.

[[link:/tools/21|Gemini]] is the least friction-heavy option if the team already lives in Google Workspace, since it works inside Gmail and Docs without a separate account.

The limit that bites: message caps and model access. Research is cheap until you are doing it daily, which is exactly what early sales requires.

## Look credible on almost nothing

This is the category where free tools deliver the most disproportionate value, because the alternative is hiring a designer.

[[link:/tools/269|Namelix]] generates brandable names with domain availability hints. It is free, it favours coined names over dictionary words, and it is fast enough to explore a dozen directions in an afternoon.

[[link:/tools/310|Looka]] turns a name into a logo, a palette and a type system, and extends the identity into social assets. Previewing is free; downloading the files requires payment. For a startup that has not raised yet, the preview is often enough to test how the brand reads on a landing page.

[[link:/tools/492|Canva AI Magic Studio]] covers everything downstream: pitch decks, one-pagers, social graphics, ad creative. Templates keep a small team's output visually consistent, which is the property investors notice without naming.

[[link:/tools/87|Gamma]] generates a deck from an outline and exports to web, PDF or PowerPoint. For a first investor deck, the draft is most of the work, and a web link is easier to update than a file attachment.

The limit that bites: asset downloads and export branding. Free tiers are generous for previewing and stingy for producing final files.

## Operate a small team

[[link:/tools/5|Notion AI]] drafts and summarises inside the workspace and answers questions across existing pages, which is what stops a five-person team from re-deciding the same thing monthly. It is only worth it if documentation already lives there.

[[link:/tools/11|Whisper]] transcribes locally with no per-minute fee, which matters when every customer call should become searchable notes. A startup having thirty conversations a week cannot pay per minute for transcripts; running the model locally makes it free.

[[link:/tools/224|Clipchamp]] handles the demo video and the product walkthrough with no subscription, which is enough for a landing page and a first sales asset.

The limit that bites: seats. Free tiers are designed for one person. The moment a second teammate needs access, the price is per head.

## The limits, collected

| Job | Free option | What ends the free tier |
|---|---|---|
| Prototype the product | [[link:/tools/98|Lovable]] | Generation credits |
| Test models | [[link:/tools/92|Hugging Face]] | Hosted inference volume |
| Market research | [[link:/tools/10|Perplexity AI]] | Daily usage caps |
| Long-document analysis | [[link:/tools/20|Claude]] | Usage limits |
| Name and identity | [[link:/tools/269|Namelix]] | Domain purchase |
| Logo files | [[link:/tools/310|Looka]] | Downloading the assets |
| Deck and graphics | [[link:/tools/87|Gamma]] | Export branding |
| Documentation | [[link:/tools/5|Notion AI]] | Seats |
| Transcripts | [[link:/tools/11|Whisper]] | Nothing, if self-hosted |

That last row is the pattern worth internalising. Open-weight tools are the only ones where the free tier does not expire, because there is no vendor to convert.

## When to start paying

Pay when a tool is on the critical path and its limit is blocking revenue, not before.

Three specific triggers justify a subscription: the product cannot ship without it, a customer-facing workflow stops working at the cap, or a teammate cannot do their job without a seat. Everything else can wait, and most of it will turn out not to be needed.

The reverse also holds. A tool that has been free for two months and is not on the critical path should be cancelled rather than upgraded, because the upgrade is a habit rather than a decision.

## The short version

Startups should optimise for free tiers that survive growth, and the ones that survive are open-weight tools and generous prototypes.

Build with generation tools, research with cited answers, present with generated decks, and run transcripts locally. Pay only when a limit blocks something that produces revenue, and prefer the tool you can host yourself when the choice is close.
